analysis.investment_thesis: Delhivery has delivered impressive revenue growth of 32.5% CAGR over six years and has just achieved its first full-year profit in FY2025, but with an operating margin of merely 0.79%, ROE of 1.52%, and a P/E of 192x, the business remains unproven as a profitable compounder. I do not buy businesses at these valuations before profitability has been established and sustained.
key_strengths: Revenue CAGR of 32.5% over six years is genuinely exceptional and reflects real market share gains in India's fast-growing e-commerce logistics ecosystem
Technology platform (OS1, TransportOne, LocateOne) creates a potential data and software moat that differentiates Delhivery from pure-play truckers — this is the kind of innovation I look for
Low Debt/Equity of 0.17 and a large equity base (INR 9,529 Cr equity) provide a strong balance sheet runway to invest through the growth phase
key_risks: Operating margin of just 0.79% after years of massive investment is deeply concerning — logistics is a brutally competitive, thin-margin industry and I see no evidence of durable pricing power yet
No identifiable promoter (VC/PE backed); FII holds 48.6% — I need to understand who the visionary operator is and what their long-term orientation looks like before committing capital
P/E of 192x and Forward P/E of 55x on embryonic profits leave no margin of safety; even a modest disappointment in margin recovery would be catastrophic for the share price
red_flags: Six consecutive years of net losses before FY2025's INR 162 Cr profit — the profit track record is essentially zero, which violates a core Fisher principle of proven earning power
OCF was positive in only 3 of the last 5 years; free cash flow just barely turned positive (INR 92 Cr in FY2025) — the cash generation story has not been validated
ROE of 1.52% and ROCE of 2.47% are essentially bank deposit returns on a massive equity base — management has yet to demonstrate capital allocation excellence
analysis.detailed_analysis: Delhivery is a genuinely interesting business and India's e-commerce logistics boom is real. The revenue growth is the kind of number I cannot ignore, and the technology platform ambition — creating an OS for supply chains — resonates with my belief that the best companies build products that customers cannot easily replicate. However, my 15-point checklist demands worthwhile profit margins and demonstrated earning power. A company that burned cash for six years and has just emerged with sub-1% operating margins has not yet earned the right to a quality valuation. I would use scuttlebutt extensively here — speaking with e-commerce companies about switching costs, with drivers about operational culture, and with competitors about Delhivery's actual price discipline. Until margins durably cross 5%+ and ROE approaches 15%, I hold this at arm's length.
